desc:
An edit script from s to t reads both strings from left to right, one step at a time. Every step is one of:

  • keep: the next characters of s and t are equal, consume both (cost 0);
  • replace: the next characters are different, consume both (cost 1);
  • delete: consume one character of s (cost 1);
  • insert: consume one character of t (cost 1).

The script ends when both strings are fully consumed. Count how many different scripts have the minimum possible total cost (the edit distance), modulo 1,000,000,007. Two scripts are different if their sequences of steps differ. When the next characters are equal, the only way to consume both together is keep.

s = "cat", t = "cut"  ->  1   (keep, replace, keep)
s = "ab",  t = "ba"   ->  3   (replace twice; delete a, keep b, insert a; insert b, keep a, delete b)
s = "a",   t = "b"    ->  1
s = "",    t = ""     ->  1   (the empty script)
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: First compute the ordinary edit distance table. A script is a monotone path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell; which paths are optimal?
Store in every cell a pair: the minimum cost to reach it and the number of different paths that achieve that minimum.

For a cell, look at its three predecessors (diagonal, above, left) with their added costs. The new minimum is the smallest total; the count is the sum of the counts of all predecessors that reach exactly that minimum. Reduce modulo 10<sup>9</sup>+7.
editorial: Every script is a path in the grid of prefix pairs (i, j): a diagonal step consumes one character of each string, a vertical step deletes, a horizontal step inserts. Keeping and replacing are the two kinds of diagonal step, chosen by whether the characters are equal. So counting optimal scripts means counting the cheapest paths in a grid with these step costs.

Each cell stores (cost, ways). To fill it, compute the three candidate costs: cost[i-1][j-1] + (0 if equal else 1), cost[i-1][j] + 1 and cost[i][j-1] + 1. The cell's cost is the smallest candidate, and its ways is the sum of ways over all predecessors whose candidate equals that smallest value, modulo 109+7. This works because the cost of a path is additive, so a cheapest path to a cell extends a cheapest path to one of its predecessors. Do not take the maximum or the minimum of counts across different costs: only predecessors that tie for the best cost are summed. Row-wise rolling arrays are enough, so the memory is linear.
solution:
def countOptimalScripts(s, t):
    MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
    n = len(t)
    prev_c = list(range(n + 1))
    prev_w = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        a = s[i - 1]
        cur_c = [i] + [0] * n
        cur_w = [1] + [0] * n
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a == t[j - 1]:
                c = prev_c[j - 1]
            else:
                c = prev_c[j - 1] + 1
            w = prev_w[j - 1]
            e = prev_c[j] + 1
            if e < c:
                c = e
                w = prev_w[j]
            elif e == c:
                w += prev_w[j]
            e = cur_c[j - 1] + 1
            if e < c:
                c = e
                w = cur_w[j - 1]
            elif e == c:
                w += cur_w[j - 1]
            cur_c[j] = c
            cur_w[j] = w % MOD
        prev_c, prev_w = cur_c, cur_w
    return prev_w[n] % MOD
